history.content: I see yellow spots that turn into white streaks on the veins of my maize leaves and the plants are short. What can I do?

This mixture treats about 1,500 to 2,000 plants per kilogram. Repeat the application every 8 to 10 days during the young stage. Do not use neem powder alone because the oil will scorch the plant; always mix it with the inert carrier. After you finish harvesting, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

history.content: My ewes are coughing and some have died fast, what must I avoid and how should I handle the dead ones?

history.content: What management should I follow for Striga hermonthica on sorghum?

history.content: The leaves of my cassava are yellow mottled and look twisted, and the plants are short. Is this mosaic disease and what actions are required?

draws.answer: Yes, those symptoms are cassava mosaic disease. No spray will cure an infected plant, so you must remove the plants that are strongly mottled and twisted. Uproot and destroy those plants immediately. For the next crop, cut only from healthy-looking cassava plants, avoiding any mottled or deformed stems. Obtain improved tolerant cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and plant them. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

Yes, those signs are cassava mosaic disease. First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant cassava variety sourced from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. No spray will cure the disease. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

per_item.reference: Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn what you uproot so seed does not spread. Then feed the soil with organic manure plus some urea to weaken Striga and strengthen the crop, and earth up the soil. After that rotate or intercrop with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. These steps reduce the thousands of seeds each plant sheds. For tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan, see ICAT.

history.content: how stop Striga seeds

draws.answer: You must avoid planting cassava or maize on the same field next season after cassava is grown. First, take cuttings only from healthy plants. Then remove any cassava or maize stems that are past the flowering stage and destroy them. After that, plant a cereal crop in that plot to break the cassava-mycessaption cycle. If you see strong white flower buds, go to ICAT for certified seed.

Striga keeps its flowers in the ground where it was sown and waits for a root to grow. First, pull the plants at 15-30 days after sowing and repeat the weeding at 20-25 days. When you see a clear pocket 2-3 weeks after sowing, drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each pocket. This treats the flower buds before the root system has been established. Do not use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the seedlings. After the flowering stage, plant a legume like cowpea or soybean to break the cycle. For a large block attacked at once, contact ICAT quickly.

per_item.reference: Photos are beyond my capability. For accurate advice, tell me exactly what you observe: highlight the section of the plant with issues, describe the color of any spots, differentiate between leaf bending and mere color change, indicate whether it emerged on old or fresh leaves, note any wilting, and whether the problems appear alone or together. This description typically narrows down the cause. If more precision is needed, I'll suggest involving ICAT for a hands-on assessment.

history.content: Can I send you a photo of my plant?

draws.answer: I cannot process images or detect plant diseases from visual cues, as I lack a specialized image analysis module. My capacity is limited to textual information, and I do not possess the capability to examine photographs. However, you can describe your plant's symptoms, its growth stage, and the surrounding ecosystem, and I will provide guidance based on my training. For any plant-related issues, I recommend you consult ICAT for a visual diagnosis.

No, and that is by design. I process text inputs, so I cannot analyze an image and provide a plant diagnosis. What I can do is give you advice on crops and animals after you have observed them directly, describing the signs in text. If you imagine a plant or an animal, describe its outward appearance, and I will tell you what to expect. For accurate identification, especially with symptoms like color variations or growth patterns, consult ICAT: they have the tools and knowledge to differentiate between diseases.

per_item.reference: It is Striga (witchweed) on your sorghum. Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn what you uproot so the seed does not spread. Then feed the soil with organic manure plus some urea and earth up the field to weaken Striga and strengthen the crop. After that rotate or intercrop with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan, see ICAT.

history.content: I see a purple weed around the base of my sorghum and the plants stay short and yellow even though it has rained well.
Is the purple weed still without flowers, or have you noticed any flower buds on it?
It has not flowered yet, I only see the purple stems.

draws.answer: You have a sorghum striga infection caused by a red or purple flowered Mucuna pr corporation. Sow a Mucuna seed mix where the sorghum stalks sit, lay three to five grains on each pocket, and bury two-thirds of each seed with the node-tops up, never lay the seed on a flat surface. Ten to fifteen days later pull the sorghum up and dig a shallow channel as shown. When the sorghum reaches flowering, tie a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel and repeat the treatment every eight to ten days, never using neem powder alone. After the sorghum flowers, cut the stems at ground level to let the root system stay in the soil. For a large block under attack, see ICAT quickly for approved control. I cannot give you the exact date for planting the sorghum.

You have a pink or purple Striga that is waiting to attach to the roots of your sorghum. First, cut the groundnut stem at ground level, leaving the nodules in the soil. Then, when the soil is still wet, drop a pinch of groundnut (or a pinch of feather powder) into each pocket where the Striga has been planted. One kilogram of the mix will cover about 1,500 to 2,000 plants, and you should repeat the treatment every eight to ten days. After the sorghum is in its early stage, pull any Striga clings from the base of the plants. For a large block of sorghum, ask ICAT for the current approved product and its exact dose.

per_item.reference: Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted weeds so the seed does not spread. Then feed the soil with organic manure plus some urea, which weakens Striga and strengthens your sorghum. Finally rotate or intercrop with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. These actions together reduce the seed that builds up in the soil. For tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan, see ICAT.

history.content: how stop Striga seed buildup

draws.answer: Stop planting Striga right after planting cowpea. First sow a resistant improved cowpea variety that matures in 55 to 75 days. Then weed the field to keep the Striga from taking root. When the cowpea plants are 30 to 35 days old and flower buds appear, pull the Striga into the soil or bury it so it cannot grow. After that, do the first application of NPK fertilizer at 150 to 200 kg per hectare, then split urea applications of 50 kg per hectare, and add 25 kg of phosphate per hectare. End by consulting ICAT for a variety that matches your grain or fodder goal.

Striga needs no water and no air to grow, so first pull it out of the soil as soon as you see it, getting the roots wrapped in a shower cloth to keep it from enturbining. Then sow certified seed that has been treated against damping-off and do not sow too thickly. Keep the nursery bed evenly moist but never soggy and stop watering late in the evening. Keep the stand clean and do not let weeds emerge. If plants still die, visit ICAT for an approved nursery drench and the correct rate.

per_item.reference: Uproot and destroy those plants and do not use any cuttings from them. After removal, select cuttings only from plants with normal leaf shape and no spots, and use a tolerant variety for replanting. This stops the spread of the virus that moves through infected cuttings and whitefly. For confirmation, go to ITRA.

history.content: Some of my cassava plants are wilting and have angular spots on the leaves. Should I keep them?

draws.answer: No, do not keep those plants. Remove and destroy them because they are affected by cassava bacterial blight. Disinfect your tools before moving to the next plant to stop spread. Use cuttings only from healthy plants that show no symptoms. Choose a resistant cassava variety for your next planting. For clean resistant cuttings, go to ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to verify the disease.

No, you must remove those plants because they are infected with cassava bacterial blight. Disinfect your tools between each plant to prevent spread. Use cuttings only from healthy plants. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot to a new site. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can help you confirm the disease.

per_item.reference: The symptom you describe is nitrogen loss in maize. First dig a shallow drainage channel so water can leave the plot instead of standing. When the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burning it. Then keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If later you notice streaks or dead-hearts, you should consult ICAT.

history.content: After yesterday's downpour my corn field has the bottom leaves turning pale, but there are no spots. What should I do?

draws.answer: The pale colour of the lower maize leaves after heavy rain means nitrogen has been leached. First, dig a shallow drainage ditch so water can leave the plot rather than pool. When the soil has drained, place urea in a small pocket 5 to 10 cm from each stem, using about 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation, and keep the granules off the plant to avoid burning. Continue with the second weeding and earthing-up as planned. If you later observe streaks or dead-hearts, you should see ICAT.

The pale colour on the lower leaves of your maize after the rain is a sign of nitrogen being washed away. First dig a shallow drainage channel so water can flow off the plot instead of standing. When the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation and keeping the fertilizer off the plant so it does not burn. Then continue with the second weeding and earthing-up at the usual time. If you later notice streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: No, those symptoms are maize streak virus. Remove the most affected plants and destroy them to cut the source of infection. After that, plan to use an MSV-tolerant variety for the next planting and ask ICAT for the right seed. Make sure you do not sow your maize late, because late sowing increases infection. For confirmation and variety advice, see ICAT.

history.content: I see some yellow spots on the leaves that become white streaks along the veins and the plants are short. Can I keep them?

draws.answer: Those signs indicate tomato yellow leaf curl virus affecting your tomato. Begin by keeping the market-garden area clean and act early to control whitefly, the insect that spreads the virus. Plant a resistant tomato variety in your next season to avoid the disease. For assistance with whitefly control and choosing a resistant variety, go to ICAT.

Those signs are caused by whiteflies and they can spread tomato yellow leaf curl virus, which leaves stay after the insects are gone. Shake a plant and look before you spray, because the wrong name wastes spray and money. Turn the leaves over and count insects on a few plants before deciding to treat. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and clear weeds around the plot edges. Use yellow sticky traps to catch adult whiteflies. For the correct product and its rate, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is maize streak virus affecting your maize, not a stalk borer. First, rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the virus source. Next season, request an improved MSV-tolerant variety from ICAT and plant it. Avoid sowing late because late planting increases infection. Neem powder will not control this disease, so do not apply it. If a large proportion of your field is infected, see ICAT promptly for confirmation and variety recommendation.

history.content: There are yellow spots that join into pale streaks along my maize leaf veins and the plants are dwarf. Should I mix neem with sand and put it in the whorls?

draws.answer: Those signs indicate maize stalk borer. While the maize plants are young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each whorl funnel; one kilogram treats about 1,500 to 2,000 plants and you must repeat the treatment every 8 to 10 days. Never apply the neem powder by itself because the oil can scorch the maize, always use the inert carrier with the mixture. After you finish harvesting, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

The maize is affected by a stalk borer. While the plants are still young, drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each whorl funnel; one kilogram will treat roughly 1,500 to 2,000 plants. Repeat the treatment every 8 to 10 days as long as the seedlings stay young. Never apply the neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant; always mix it with the inert carrier. After harvesting, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in rotation. If a large area is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

per_item.reference: You have cassava brown streak disease, which shows yellow blotches or chlorosis along leaf veins and a brown, corky necrotic rot inside the roots. Use cuttings only from plants that have no yellow blotches and no root rot, and choose a tolerant variety for new planting. Uproot and destroy any plants that show the yellow leaf veins or brown root rot, and do not take cuttings from those affected areas. Because the disease is not well documented in Togo, have ITRA confirm the diagnosis and check the root symptoms. If you need further help, contact ITRA.

history.content: I think something is wrong with my cassava, the leaves look odd and the roots seem soft.
Are you seeing yellow blotches along the leaf veins or a brown, corky rot inside the roots?
Yes, the leaves have yellow streaks on the veins and when I pull up a plant the root is brown and corky.

draws.answer: You have cassava bacterial blight. Use cuttings only from plants that have no symptoms. Remove and destroy every affected plant. Disinfect your tools between each plant. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot to a different site. For clean resistant cuttings you can contact ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.

You have cassava bacterial blight caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis. Use only cuttings taken from healthy plants for planting. Remove and destroy any affected plants you find. Disinfect your tools between each plant. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot to a new site. For clean resistant cuttings you should contact ITRA or a registered producer.

per_item.reference: You are dealing with peste des petits ruminants (PPR). Isolate every sick animal at once and STOP all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals for market during the outbreak and dispose of carcasses safely. Support the sick animals with water and soft feed. Vaccinate the healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: My goats have been coughing a lot and some have died very quickly.
Do they also have fever and a mucky discharge from the nose or eyes?
Yes, they have fever and a mucky discharge from the nose and eyes.

draws.answer: You are dealing with a tick-borne disease that destroys red blood cells, which makes the gums turn pale. Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can tell which disease it is and give the right drug and dose. Mention the urine colour to the vet; red or black suggests redwater, yellow-brown without red suggests gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not only on the sick animal. Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service will provide the proper treatment.

Your goats are infected with a tick-borne disease that destroys red blood cells, which makes the animal look pale. Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can tell which disease it is and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; red or black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick goat in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just on the sick goat. Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service will provide the appropriate medication.

per_item.reference: It is groundnut leaf spot that is affecting your peanuts. First, do not plant groundnut on that field again next season; rotate the plot with cereals. Then choose a tolerant groundnut variety and make sure you clear or bury any remaining groundnut residues from the previous crop. After that, harvest the groundnut as soon as it is ready so the weakened plants do not lose their pods early. These actions will break the cycle of the Cercospora leaf-spot fungus that lives in crop residues and spreads in humid conditions. For advice on resistant varieties or whether a fungicide is needed, see ICAT.

history.content: My peanuts are dropping their leaves fast and I see dark circles on them. Could this be leaf spot and what should I do?

draws.answer: Yes, those signs are typical of groundnut leaf spot, which appears as dark round spots and early leaf drop. First, stop planting groundnut on that land in the next season to break the disease cycle. Then rotate the field with cereals for the next planting season. After that, select a tolerant groundnut variety and clear or bury all the old groundnut residues in the soil. Also, harvest the groundnut crop at the right time so weakened plants do not lose pods early. For advice on resistant varieties and whether a fungicide is needed, see ICAT.

Yes, those symptoms are typical of groundnut leaf spot caused by Cercospora fungi. Begin by rotating your groundnut with cereals to stop the fungus from persisting in the soil. Then, use a tolerant groundnut variety and clear or bury all old groundnut residues after harvest. After that, harvest your groundnut on time because a weakened crop drops its pods early. For advice on resistant varieties or the need for a fungicide, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: The chlorotic spots and broken white streaks are signs of maize streak virus, which is spread by leafhoppers. Start by rogueing out and destroying the most severely affected maize plants to cut the source. After that, plan to plant an improved MSV-tolerant variety next season; ask ICAT for the appropriate seed. Avoid late sowing because it raises infection. No spray can cure an infected plant. For disease confirmation and variety selection, see ICAT.

history.content: There are tiny green insects on my maize and the leaves show chlorotic spots with broken white streaks. How do I deal with this?

draws.answer: Those spots and streaks are a sign of maize stalk borer on maize. While the plants are still young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each whorl funnel. Never apply neem powder alone because the oil will scorch the maize. One kilogram of this mixture will treat roughly 1,500 to 2,000 plants. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

per_item.reference: No, do not mix two products to make the spray stronger. Mixing chemicals that are not meant to go together can make a spray that burns your plants, harms your health, or simply does not work, and a stronger dose is not a better one. Use one approved product at a time, at the dose written on its label. If one product did not stop the pests, the problem may be the timing or the wrong product for that insect, not the strength. Ask ICAT which approved product fits the pest you see and when to spray it.

history.content: Would mixing two different insecticides give a stronger spray?

draws.answer: Using two different insecticides does not make a spray stronger. The reason is that the insecticide's mode of action is separate, and together they cover the insect's various vulnerabilities. One spray covers the insects that carry the disease, while the second sprays those that transmit it. If you mix them, you would need to identify which insect is the carrier and select the right product. For the correct product and its application rate, go to ICAT.

No, you should not mix two different insecticides because that can cause a wrong product and reduce its effectiveness. First, look at the labels of the insecticides you plan to use and note their active ingredients and recommended rates. Then use only the product that is labeled for the specific pest on your crop. Next, drop the insecticide onto the plant and keep it off, shaking and measuring as you go. If you need help choosing the right product, contact ICAT.

per_item.reference: You are dealing with a peste des petits ruminants (PPR) outbreak. Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals for market during the outbreak and dispose of carcasses safely. Give the sick animals plenty of clean water and soft feed to support them. Vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: My goats have been coughing and some have fever.
Are you also seeing muco-purulent discharge from the nose or eyes, or sores inside the mouth?
Yes, they have a thick yellow discharge from the nose and some have sores in the mouth.

draws.answer: It is Newcastle disease. Isolate every surviving animal from the sick ones and do not move, sell or gift any animal. Burn or bury dead animals and any soiled litter, then disinfect the house thoroughly. Vaccinate the remaining herd with the La Sota or B1 strain in water or as eye-drops and follow the repeat schedule. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately for help.

You are dealing with a cattle tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, transmitted by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify the specific disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, as yellow-brown suggests gall sickness and red-black suggests redwater. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water nearby and avoid making it walk because it is low on red blood cells. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick animal, to prevent further spread. Never use the same needle on two animals because gall sickness can be transmitted that way. See the veterinary service for diagnosis and proper treatment.

per_item.reference: Your sorghum is suffering from Striga, the witchweed that parasitises the roots. Remove the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn the removed plants to avoid seed spread. After weeding, apply organic manure together with some urea and earth-up the soil, because this combination weakens Striga and helps sorghum grow stronger. Then rotate or intercrop with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to reduce the soil seed bank. For tolerant sorghum varieties and a multi-year rotation plan for severely infested fields, visit ICAT.

history.content: Why are my sorghum plants short and yellow while I see a pink flowered weed at their base?

draws.answer: Your sorghum is suffering from nitrogen shortage in a soil that has lost organic matter. First, stop buying broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer and systemic fungicide because they will not solve the nitrogen deficiency. Second, restore organic matter by applying manure, compost, or by leaving or burying the sorghum residues instead of burning them. Third, plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Fourth, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose for your plot before any large purchase. ICAT can help you with the analysis.

The short stature and yellow leaves of your sorghum are because of nitrogen depletion in a soil that has lost organic matter from continuous cropping without returning residues. First, stop buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer and a systemic fungicide; they will not restore yield on a run-down plot. Second, bring organic matter back by applying manure, using compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Third, rotate with a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Fourth, go to ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper fertilizer dose for your plot. ICAT is the service to see.

per_item.reference: No spray will cure an infected plant, so you must act on the plants. First, walk the field and identify chlorotic spots that turn into broken pale or white streaks along the veins and any stunted growth; these are signs of maize streak virus carried by leafhoppers. Then rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source of infection. After the harvest, plan to plant an improved MSV-tolerant variety for the next season and ask ICAT for the recommended seed. Also avoid sowing late, because late sowing raises infection risk. If a large share of your field is affected, go to ICAT to confirm the disease and get the tolerant variety recommendation.

history.content: How should I manage maize streak virus in my maize field?

draws.answer: The everyday name is maize streak virus. First, detect the presence of yellow or pale streaks along the veins of the leaves. Next, keep the plot clean and act early to control any whitefly that could spread the virus. Then, plant a tolerant maize variety in the next season to reduce future risk. For detailed whitefly control and whether a tolerant variety is recommended, see ICAT.

The everyday name for maize streak virus is "maize streak virus". First, check for yellow or pale streaks along leaf veins while moving through the field. If you see those patterns, treat with a strong jet of water to the leaves. Next, shake each plant and look for a cloud of tiny white insects that rise and settle back down. Pull out the most infested leaves and destroy them, and clear weeds around the plot edges. Use yellow sticky traps to catch adult whiteflies and spray a strong jet of water on aphids, letting ladybirds and lacewings help. If the infestation is heavy, contact ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

per_item.reference: There is no cure once groundnut rosette is present. Remove and destroy any severely affected plants to stop spread. Plant your next crop early and use the recommended close spacing, because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field completely weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that transmit the virus. Choose a tolerant variety for the next season to lower risk. Remember that leaf spot shows dark round spots and is a different problem. For resistant varieties, contact ICAT.

history.content: My groundnut leaves look strange and the plants are not growing well.
Do you see stunted plants with yellow or green mottling and bunched, distorted young leaves?
Yes, the leaves are mottled and the plants are short and twisted.

draws.answer: You have groundnut leaf spot caused by Cercospora fungi. Do not grow groundnut on the same land year after year, rotate with cereals. Use a tolerant variety and clear or bury old groundnut trash. Harvest on time because a weakened crop drops its pods. For variety guidance and fungicide advice, see ICAT.

You have groundnut leaf spot caused by Cercospora fungi. Do not grow groundnut on the same field year after year; rotate the field with cereals. Use a tolerant groundnut variety and clear or bury all old groundnut residues before planting the next season. Harvest the crop on time because a weakened crop will drop its pods early. For resistant seed you can contact ICAT or ITRA.

per_item.reference: Look at the symptoms on the leaves and stem. Stalk borer makes window-pane holes in the whorl leaves and a dead-heart where the central shoot dies while outer leaves stay alive; you may also see caterpillars and frass inside the stem. Maize streak virus shows chlorotic spots that join into pale or white streaks along the veins and the whole plant is stunted, without tunnels or dead-heart. If you see leaf streaks and no dead-heart, it is the virus; if you see dead-heart and holes, it is the borer. For confirmation and advice, see ICAT.

history.content: How can I tell the difference between stalk borer damage and maize streak virus in my field?

draws.answer: Stalk borer damage shows holes or punctures along the stem's interior, while maize streak virus gives yellow or pale streaks along leaf veins. Look for the borer holes on the stem and decide if you need to spray for borers, or check for the streaks on the leaves. For borer problems, use a resistant variety and destroy old plants. For streaks, rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. See ICAT for approved control methods.

Stalk borer damage shows holes or tunnels in the stems, while maize streak virus gives streaks along the veins. Look for tunnels or dead-hearts in the stems; if you see those signs, you should destroy the affected plants. After that, count the streaks on several plants before treating; if the streaks are widespread, use the approved fungicide at the rate ICAT provides. For the fungicide, go to ICAT to get the approved product and rate.

per_item.reference: Do not sow your maize late, because late sowing raises infection. After planting, walk the field and remove the worst-affected plants, pulling them out and destroying them to cut the source of the virus. For the next season, obtain an improved MSV-tolerant variety and plant it. If a large share of your field is affected, go to ICAT to confirm the disease and to get a recommendation for a tolerant variety.

history.content: How can I prevent maize streak virus in my maize field?

draws.answer: Use a resistant improved variety that matures in 55 to 75 days and sow it when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. Do the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. Spray an approved fungicide three times during the flowering stage: first at 30-35 days when buds appear, second ten days later, and third ten days after that, following the label rate. The three sprays cover the virus and its tomato-like symptoms. Consult ICAT for the current approved product and exact dose before spraying.

Use a resistant maize variety that matures in 55-75 days and sow it when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. If you face a sudden large block of healthy plants, apply an approved fungicide at about 500 g per hectare, improve drainage and airflow, and plant a tolerant variety. For confirmation of the disease and the exact fungicide rate, visit ICAT.

Also, be sure not to sow your maize late because late sowing increases the chance of infection. For disease confirmation and variety advice, visit ICAT.

history.content: My corn leaves are turning yellowish with white lines on the veins and the stalks are very short. What do I do?

draws.answer: Those signs are caused by maize stalk borer. While the plants are still young, place a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel. This treats about 1,500 to 2,000 plants per kilogram of powder and you must repeat the treatment every 8 to 10 days. Never use neem powder alone because the oil will scorch the plant; always mix it with the inert carrier. After you finish harvesting, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and then rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If many plants are affected at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

Those signs are a typical symptom of maize stalk borer. While the plants are still young, place a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel. This mix treats about 1,500-2,000 plants per kilogram, so use enough to cover the whole field. One kilogram of the mixture can treat roughly 1,500-2,000 plants, so measure the amount you need. history.content: How can I prevent Striga on my sorghum field?

draws.answer: Striga is prevented by sowing a resistant improved variety that matures in 55-75 days. Plant the seed on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five grains per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Two to three weeks later thin the stand to two or three plants per pocket and do the first weeding without breaking the ridges. After weeding, apply NPK fertilizer at 150 to 200 kilograms per hectare, then add urea at 50 to 100 kilograms per hectare, and earth up against lodging. Keep Striga away from the sorghum by not planting it in the same area next season. For a variety that fits your prefecture's rains, see ICAT.

history.content: maize streak virus symptoms what

draws.answer: Maize streak virus shows yellow or pale streaks along the leaf veins, with spots where veins end, and you see many tiny insects on the underside of the leaves. First shake the plant and look before you spray, because the wrong name wastes spray and money. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before deciding to treat. Pick the most infested leaves, destroy them and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. Use yellow sticky traps to catch adult whiteflies and a strong jet of water to knock off aphids, letting ladybirds and lacewings help. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. I cannot give you the exact product or dose.

The disease is called maize streak virus. Look for yellow or pale streaks along leaf veins that look like streaks, which points to the virus. First, confirm the virus before buying any spray; it is not a disease but a virus that requires a different strategy. Then, up your planting density to keep rows and pockets closer, which can reduce the window for transmission. Next, plant a resistant improved 55-75 day variety to limit the outbreak. Finally, control whitefly populations by keeping the plot clean and using yellow sticky traps for insects. For the correct product and dose, go to ICAT.

history.content: My maize shows chlorotic spots that turn into broken pale streaks along the veins and the plants are stunted. What should I do?

draws.answer: The problem is nitrogen depletion in your maize crop. Begin by reading the leaves: a uniform pale yellow on older leaves signals nitrogen hunger, not a disease. Then, do not rely only on mineral fertilizer because on run-down soil it often does not pay off. Next, bring back organic matter by spreading manure, adding compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. After that, plant a legume like soybean, groundnut or cowpea in the next rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose for your plot.

Those signs are nitrogen loss after rain, not a disease. Open a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of staying. When the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, keeping it off the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later see pale streaks on veins or dead-heart symptoms, go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: That is maize streak virus, a disease of maize that appears as chlorotic spots turning into pale streaks along the veins and causes stunted growth. Remove and destroy the worst-affected maize plants right away to cut the source of the virus. In the next planting season, use an improved MSV-tolerant maize variety and request the appropriate seed from ICAT. Plant your maize early, because late sowing raises the chance of infection. To confirm the disease and get the tolerant seed recommendation, go to ICAT.

history.content: The maize in my field has yellow-white streaks on the leaves and they are not growing tall; I think it's the bugs.

draws.answer: You are dealing with a maize stalk borer problem caused by Busseola fusca or Chilo partellus. While the plants are still young, place a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel. One kilogram of this mixture will treat about 1,500 to 2,000 plants, so use enough to cover the whole field. Repeat the application every 8 to 10 days until the crop reaches the flowering stage. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large area is heavily attacked, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

It is not Maize stalk borer, it is a nitrogen loss because the yellow-white streaks on the whorl leaves and lack of height are signs of nitrogen hunger, not a pest. The pest causes window-pane holes on the whorl and tip leaves and the stalk stays tall. To treat the pest, split and discard the heavily affected leaves, and also add manure or compost each year to rebuild soil organic matter. Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's advice. For the next crop, plant a legume like cowpea or groundnut. For advice on the correct fertilizer dose for your plot, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: This is groundnut rosette. Start by roguing out and destroying the severely affected plants. Then plant the next groundnut crop early and follow the recommended close spacing to obtain a dense stand. Keep the field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that carry the virus. Use a tolerant groundnut variety in the following season. For resistant variety options, see ICAT.

history.content: My groundnut field has plants that are short, with yellow mottled leaves and distorted young leaves. What steps must I take?

draws.answer: Those plants are showing groundnut leaf spot, so you need to rogue out the badly affected groundnut. Pull out and destroy the plants that are short and have yellow mottling and twisted leaves. Then, when you replant, select a tolerant groundnut variety. Also, do not grow groundnut on the same land in consecutive seasons; rotate with cereals instead. If you need help choosing a tolerant variety or calculating a rotation interval, go to ICAT.

Those plants are typical of groundnut leaf spot. Do not grow groundnut on the same plot year after year; rotate with cereals to break the disease cycle. Plant a tolerant groundnut variety and clear or bury all old groundnut trash after harvest. Harvest the new crop on time to avoid weakened plants dropping pods early. For advice on resistant varieties or whether a fungicide is needed, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: The problem is cassava brown streak disease, so use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. First, walk through your field and identify any plants with yellow blotches on the leaves or brown, corky rot in the roots. Uproot those affected plants and destroy them, making sure not to move any cuttings from those areas. Do not use any cuttings from the infected parts because the disease spreads by infected cuttings and whitefly. Finally, take a sample to ITRA for confirmation since this disease is not well documented in Togo.

history.content: My cassava leaves look a bit strange and the roots seem soft, what should I do?
Do you see yellow blotches or chlorosis along the leaf veins?
Yes, the leaves have yellow streaks along the veins.

draws.answer: You have cassava mosaic disease. No spray will cure an infected cassava plant, so you must remove the problem plants. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and will keep feeding the whitefly that spreads the virus. For the next planting, take cuttings only from plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can help you.

Then for the next crop, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If the symptoms are angular spots with wilting instead of leaf deformation, go to ICAT for confirmation; for clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

per_item.reference: It is not heartwater, it is PPR virus that causes the muco-purulent discharge, fever and rapid deaths. Heartwater looks similar but needs a lab test to confirm. With PPR you must isolate sick animals, stop movement, give water and soft feed, avoid selling or slaughtering, and notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: is it heartwater causing the muco-purulent discharge

draws.answer: It is not heartwater, it is African swine fever. Heartwater shows a swollen left flank and is a different disease, while African swine fever shows high fever, red blotches, bloody diarrhoea, and rapid death in many animals. Because it is African swine fever, there is no treatment or vaccine and you must confine all pigs, stop any pig movement, keep visitors away, disinfect the pen, install a footbath, boil food scraps, and safely bury or burn dead pigs. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

It is not fowl pox, it is the wet form caused by the dry form infected with the dry form's virus. Fowl pox shows scabs or lesions and progresses faster, while wet fowl pox shows lesions that start as wart-like spots and develop into the wet form you described. Because it is the wet form, you must remove any remaining trees, clean the area, and disinfect thoroughly. Isolate any birds with raised wart-like scabs, give them extra feed and water, and consider treatment for the wet form. For the dry form, you should contact ICAT for diagnosis and treatment.

per_item.reference: The Striga on sorghum leaves many seeds in the soil, so the seed bank grows over time. Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted weeds to stop more seeds from spreading. Then add organic manure together with a little urea and earth up to weaken the Striga and help the sorghum grow. After that, rotate or intercrop your sorghum with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to deplete the seed bank. If the field is heavily infested, go to ICAT for tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: Why does the witchweed keep coming back in my sorghum plot?

draws.answer: Witchweed keeps returning because it is the same plant that hosts stalk borer larvae. Plant a cereal after the soybean so the cereal benefits from the nitrogen the soybean provides. Cut the soybean stems at ground level and leave the nitrogen-fixing root nodules in the soil. After soybean harvest, clear or bury all old sorghum residue to stop the weed from being re-sown. Then sow a cereal in the same field to capture the pest before it spreads. If you need help matching a variety or deciding on a product, go to ICAT.

The sorghum is being taken over by witchweed. First, stop planting sorghum on the same field for more than two years consecutively, which cuts the weed pressure. Then, when the sorghum is at panicle initiation, apply a Fongorene-type seed treatment at 6 g per kilogram of seed. After that, if a large block of sorghum shows symptoms, use an approved benomyl-type fungicide at roughly 500 g per hectare, improve drainage and airflow, and plant a tolerant variety. For the exact current fungicide and rate, go to ICAT to obtain the approved product and its precise dosage.
